To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Experiential Avoidence and Rumination in parents of children with cancer were positively related with Posttraumatic stress and Depression.

experiential avoidance and rumination are related to posttraumatic stress symptoms and symptoms of depression and that rumination and experiential avoidance explain additional variance in symptoms of posttraumatic stress and symptoms of depression over that explained by symptoms.

Experiential avoidance (i.e., a tendency to avoid unpleasant thoughts and feelings) and rumination (i.e., repetitive and passive thinking) are related to posttraumatic stress symptoms (i.e., intrusive memories of the traumatic event, avoidance of thoughts and feelings about the event, and symptoms of hyperarousal and negative affect) and symptoms of depression (i.e., low positive affect and low life satisfaction) in parents of children diagnosed with cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the psychological processes involved in the adjustment of parents whose children are on cancer treatment.
the relationship between experiental avoidance, rumination, posttraumatic stress symptoms, and symptoms of depression among parents of children on treatment for cancer.
the psychological processes that may be important for the understanding and treatment of PTSS and depressive symptoms in parents of children with cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

experiential avoidance is a predictor of symptoms of depression, whereas rumination is a predictor of both posttraumatic stress symptoms and symptoms of depression among parents of children with cancer.
rumination and EA are related to both PTSS and symptoms depression in parents of a child on cancer treatment.
EA and rumination are important constructs in understanding the development of PTSS and depression in parents of cancer patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
rumination and experiential avoidance are important constructs in understanding the development and maintenance of posttraumatic stress and depressive symptoms in parents of children with cancer.
experiential avoidance and rumination are important constructs in understanding post-traumatic stress and depression in parents of paediatric cancer patients.
experiential avoidance and rumination are important constructs in our understanding of posttraumatic stress symptoms and symptoms of depression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
experiential avoidance and rumination are important factors to consider in the understanding of psychological distress in parents of children with cancer.
experiential avoidance and rumination should be considered when treating parents of children on treatment for cancer.
experiential avoidance is a significant predictor of symptoms of depression in this sample of parents of children on treatment for cancer.
